questions.stem: About electrophysiology in medicine:
options: Electroneuromyography studies peripheral nerves and muscles
Electroencephalography records brain activity; its failure can cause epilepsy
Cardiac ablation destroys tissue that generates or conducts abnormal rhythms
Electrocardiography records the heart rhythm; its disorders are arrhythmias
questions.explanation: A pacemaker delivers impulses to support the rhythm; ablation destroys tissue that generates or conducts abnormal rhythms.

questions.stem: About the functional zones of a neuron:
options: Nodes of Ranvier are where the action potential is regenerated
The axon hillock and initial segment form the trigger zone, rich in NaV channels, where the AP is initiated
Myelin is made by oligodendrocytes in the peripheral nervous system
Dendrites produce graded potentials
questions.explanation: Myelin: Schwann cells in the PNS, oligodendrocytes in the CNS. Nodes of Ranvier are rich in NaV channels (saltatory conduction).

questions.stem: A patient has a demyelinating neuropathy. Nerve conduction studies may show:
options: Faster conduction because the AP has fewer internodes to cross
Reduced conduction velocity
Conduction block with a drop in response amplitude
Prolonged latencies
questions.explanation: Loss of myelin slows conduction and can block it: reduced velocity, prolonged latencies or a drop in amplitude across the affected segment.

questions.stem: About the types of membrane potential:
options: A graded potential has a constant amplitude whatever the stimulus
A pacemaker potential is a spontaneous depolarization towards threshold, as in the sinoatrial node
Slow waves are typical of the sinoatrial node
The resting potential of a typical neuron is about −70 mV
questions.explanation: Graded potentials (EPSP, IPSP, receptor potential) are local and their amplitude varies with the stimulus; the all-or-none signal is the action potential.

questions.stem: About resting membrane potential values:
options: Red blood cell ≈ −90 mV
A negative resting potential is enough to make a cell excitable
Skeletal muscle fibre ≈ −85 to −90 mV
Cardiac pacemaker cells have no stable resting potential
questions.explanation: All cells have a membrane potential. Excitable cells are usually more negative, but excitability depends on the types of channel, not on the RMP value alone.

questions.stem: About the ion distribution at rest:
options: A voltage needs both unequal concentrations and selective permeability
Na⁺, Cl⁻ and free Ca²⁺ are concentrated outside
Impermeant anions (proteins) are concentrated inside
K⁺ is concentrated inside the cell
questions.explanation: A concentration difference creates no voltage unless the membrane lets one ion cross more easily than others: the RMP needs gradients + selective permeability.

questions.stem: Using the Nernst equation at 37 °C, with [Na⁺]out = 145 mM and [Na⁺]in = 15 mM, the Na⁺ equilibrium potential is about:
options: +61 mV
−90 mV
−61 mV
questions.explanation: E = 61.5 × log10(145/15) ≈ 61.5 × 0.99 ≈ +61 mV. Positive because Na⁺ (z = +1) is more concentrated outside; +125 mV is ECa, −90 mV is EK.

questions.stem: About the equilibrium potential of an ion:
options: At equilibrium, the chemical and electrical forces on the ion are equal and opposite
For Ca²⁺, z = +2 halves the factor (≈ 30.8 mV)
At equilibrium, the ion stops crossing the membrane
For Cl⁻, z = −1 reverses the sign of the equation
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the gradient still exists and ions still cross in both directions, at equal rates: there is no net movement.

questions.stem: At Vm = −70 mV, with the channels open:
options: K⁺ has a driving force of about −20 mV and enters
Na⁺ has a driving force of about −131 mV and enters strongly
Cl⁻ enters strongly
Ca²⁺ enters very strongly
questions.explanation: Driving force = Vm − Eion. For Cl⁻ (Eion ≈ −66 mV) it is −4 mV: a weak outward movement, because anions move opposite to the current.

questions.stem: Why is the resting potential about −70 mV?
options: A small Na⁺ leak pulls it slightly towards ENa
The electrogenic Na⁺/K⁺ pump directly adds a few millivolts of negativity
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are open at rest
K⁺ leak conductance dominates at rest, so the RMP lies close to EK
questions.explanation: At rest NaV channels are closed (available). The RMP comes from pump-maintained gradients, PK ≫ PNa and trapped intracellular anions (Gibbs–Donnan).

questions.stem: The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz (GHK) equation:
options: Shows that the most permeant ion pulls Vm towards its own equilibrium potential
Gives the membrane potential for several permeant ions, weighted by their permeabilities
Gives the equilibrium potential of a single ion
With PK : PNa = 1 : 0.05 and mammalian values, gives about −90 mV
questions.explanation: The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential of one ion; the GHK equation gives Vm when several ions are permeant.

questions.stem: A patient with rhabdomyolysis develops hyperkalaemia. Which statements are correct?
options: The resting membrane potential depolarizes
The membrane hyperpolarizes
EK becomes less negative
Prolonged depolarization inactivates NaV channels and reduces excitability
questions.explanation: Hyperkalaemia → less negative EK → RMP depolarizes → NaV inactivation → arrhythmias and muscle weakness. Hyperpolarization is the effect of hypokalaemia.

questions.stem: About the phases of a neuronal action potential:
options: Afterhyperpolarization: KV channels stay open and close slowly
Repolarization: NaV channels are inactivated and KV channels open, K⁺ leaves
Return to rest: leak channels and the pump maintain the gradients
Depolarization: NaV channels open, Na⁺ enters and Vm moves towards ENa
questions.explanation: NaV activation is fast; KV (delayed rectifier) activation is delayed. The peak (≈ +30 mV) is limited by NaV inactivation and the delayed K⁺ current.

questions.stem: About the rising phase of the action potential:
options: The loop is stopped by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Depolarization opens more NaV channels, Na⁺ enters and depolarizes further (positive feedback)
The loop is stopped by NaV inactivation and the delayed opening of KV channels
The AP reflects a change in permeability, first to Na⁺, then to K⁺
questions.explanation: The regenerative loop is ended by NaV inactivation and delayed KV opening; the pump only maintains the gradients at rest.

questions.stem: In a voltage-clamp experiment with a step to 0 mV:
options: With TTX, the late outward current remains
With TEA, the late outward current is absent
By convention, the inward Na⁺ current is drawn upwards
With TEA, the early transient inward current disappears
questions.explanation: TTX blocks NaV (early inward INa disappears), TEA blocks KV (late outward IK). Convention: inward current downwards (negative), outward upwards.

questions.stem: About the voltage-gated Na⁺ channel (NaV):
options: Its voltage sensor is the S4 segment of each domain
At rest it is closed but available
It inactivates within about 1 ms
An inactivated channel can reopen at once if the stimulus is strong enough
questions.explanation: An inactivated NaV cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes: this is the basis of the absolute refractory period.

questions.stem: NaV versus KV channels:
options: The voltage sensor is the S4 segment in both channels
Both have six transmembrane segments (S1–S6) per domain or subunit
KV is made of 4 separate α subunits around a central pore
NaV is one α subunit with 4 homologous domains (I–IV)
questions.explanation: KV (delayed rectifier) has delayed activation and little fast inactivation, giving a slower, sustained outward current.

questions.stem: A neuron receives a suprathreshold stimulus that is then made stronger:
options: The action potential becomes larger
The action potential keeps the same amplitude
The firing frequency increases
A subthreshold stimulus would only give a local graded potential that fades
questions.explanation: All-or-none: above threshold the AP is stereotyped; stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency, not AP size.

questions.stem: About the refractory periods:
options: The relative refractory period limits the maximum firing frequency
During the relative refractory period, a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed
The relative refractory period is due to all NaV channels being open
During the absolute refractory period, no stimulus can trigger an AP, however strong
questions.explanation: Relative refractory period: some NaV still inactivated and K⁺ conductance still high (membrane hyperpolarized). Refractoriness keeps propagation one-way.

questions.stem: About tetrodotoxin and local anaesthetics:
options: Both block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Tetrodotoxin poisoning causes paralysis
Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks Na⁺ channels
Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels
questions.explanation: Lidocaine and TTX block NaV and stop conduction; TEA blocks K⁺ channels.

questions.stem: An axon is stimulated and the AP is recorded 20 mm and 50 mm from the stimulus, with latencies of 1.0 ms and 2.5 ms. The conduction velocity is:
options: 30 m/s
50 m/s
2 m/s
20 m/s
questions.explanation: v = distance difference / latency difference = 30 mm / 1.5 ms = 20 mm/ms = 20 m/s.

questions.stem: About the conduction of the action potential:
options: C fibres are fast myelinated motor fibres
Continuous conduction in unmyelinated axons costs more energy
In myelinated axons it is saltatory, at about 2–120 m/s
A stimulus applied in the middle of an axon sends APs in both directions
questions.explanation: C fibres (slow pain, autonomic) are unmyelinated, ≈ 0.5–2 m/s. Normally the refractory segment behind the AP keeps it moving forward only.

questions.stem: Which change increases conduction velocity?
options: A larger axon diameter
A smaller axon diameter
Loss of myelin
A lower temperature
questions.explanation: A larger diameter lowers internal resistance; myelin and higher temperature also speed conduction.

questions.stem: Graded potentials compared with action potentials:
options: Action potentials depend mainly on ligand-gated channels
Graded potentials can depolarize or hyperpolarize
Action potentials summate
Graded potentials have no threshold and no refractory period
questions.explanation: Only graded potentials summate (temporal, spatial); APs are always depolarizing and use voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels.

questions.stem: Two EPSPs arrive at the same synapse close together in time, and the result reaches threshold at the initial segment:
options: This is spatial summation
Summation takes place at the trigger zone (initial segment)
IPSPs arriving at the same time would subtract
This is temporal summation
questions.explanation: Temporal summation = successive inputs at the same synapse; spatial = different synapses at the same time. EPSPs add and IPSPs subtract at the initial segment.
